slots.title: U.S. cash session — Oct. 10, 2026
slots.body:
U.S. equities finished higher across the major benchmarks, with coverage tying the tone to easing concern after remarks that the U.S. would not strike Iran before the midterm elections, reducing fear of a wider Middle East conflict and related energy disruption.

The S&P 500 rose 0.6% to 7,811.54, up 46.18 points from 7,765.36, with an intraday span of 7,779.34 to 7,820.57.

The Nasdaq Composite matched that 0.6% gain, closing at 27,366.17 (+172.83), while the Dow Jones Industrial Average led among the big three at +0.8%, finishing at 51,654.95 (+423.31).

The Russell 2000 added 0.5% to 2,806.98, and the CBOE Volatility Index fell 3.7% to 14.84 (−0.57 from 15.41), the lowest close level in that cross-asset set for the day.

Megacap leadership included:
- $AMZN +3.3% to 262.43
- $MSFT +2.4% to 535.07
- $V +2.8% to 385.45
- $TSLA +2.1% to 382.70

$JNJ rose 1.9% to 261.44 and $LLY added 0.8% to 1,179.27.

Megacap decliners included $AAPL −1.1% to 336.64, $HD −1.6% to 290.74, $NFLX −1.8% to 70.30, and $TSM −1.0% to 453.31; $NVDA slipped 0.5% to 229.28 on very heavy volume (84.3M shares in the feed).

Telecom stood out on the downside among liquid actives: $T −9.8% to 22.18 and $VZ −8.7% to 41.65, far wider moves than most other large-cap names in the dataset.

Gold futures (GCUSD) rose 1.4% to 4,216.30 (+59.30), Brent crude (BZUSD) added 0.4% to 104.72, and the UUP dollar proxy ticked up 0.1% to 29.02; Bitcoin (BTCUSD) was roughly flat at 82,616.42 (+0.1%).

The latest Treasury snapshot in the feed (dated 2026-10-08) showed the 10-year yield at 5.2% and the 2s10s spread at 0.47 percentage points; no new U.S. economic releases were listed in the session economic calendar block.

Overseas indexes in the bundle included the FTSE 100 +1.1% at 10,552.05 and the Hang Seng +0.3% at 24,211.30; the Nikkei 225 was essentially unchanged at 69,030.92.

Sector ETF performance was not populated in the injected sector array for this close, and the earnings calendar block carried no reported actuals for the session.

Commentary in the news set noted stocks “back in rally mode” after a brief AI-related selloff and flagged bank and chipmaker reports plus inflation data as items on the calendar for the week ahead—describing scheduled events, not outcomes.

slots.body:

slots.title: September CPI prints Tuesday 12:30 p.m.
slots.body:

Headline inflation is expected up 3.6% from a year ago; August was 3.4%.

Month-over-month headline CPI carries a 0.6% estimate versus 0.4% prior.

“Core” inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, is estimated at 2.5% year-over-year after 2.4%.

Core month-over-month is estimated at 0.2% after 0.3%.

The release resolves how the September price level compares with what economists modeled before the print.

Do you track headline CPI or core CPI more closely month to month?

slots.title: September retail sales due Wednesday
slots.body:
Wednesday, Oct. 15, the Census Bureau’s September retail sales report is on the calendar.

Headline retail sales month-over-month are estimated at 0.2%; August was 1.4%.

Retail sales excluding autos are estimated up 0.5% month-over-month; August was 1.4%.

A separate 1:30 p.m.
ET line shows retail sales ex gas and autos estimated at 0.2% month-over-month after 1.2%.

Year-over-year retail sales carry a 5.2% estimate versus 6.0% prior.

The same morning also schedules producer prices (PPI) and weekly jobless claims at 12:30 p.m.
ET—wholesale inflation and layoff filings in one window.

Which September spending slice matters more to you—headline retail or ex-autos?
